title: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
author: Reuters
text:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.

Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).

The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.

Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .

Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.

Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.

Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.

Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

title: Celtics 107, Knicks 103: “I took the over at 58. Still alive.”
author: Russell Richardson
text:
The Knicks (0-2) traveled to Boston to face the Celtics (1-1) at TD Garden tonight. Each team was fighting for their first win of the season, and clearly pride was on the line. Through the first half, the game teetered to and fro, but the home team gained momentum in the third quarter. After falling behind by 12 in the fourth, New York fought back to a one-point deficit, but, in what felt like a postseason game, Jayson Tatum went on a heater and carried his team to victory, 107-103.

What else is there to say about Mitchell Robinson (4 PTS, 4 RBS, 22 MIN) in a green jersey? It’s a bummer. We keep it moving. Mitch had a lackluster first outing with his new team and started mediocre tonight, too. He managed to put back his own miss over OG Anunoby (20 PTS, 10 RBS, 8 AST), but two fouls sat him after three minutes.

Tatum (36 PTS, 9 RBS, 7 AST) and Paul George (15 PTS, 7 RBS) got the C’s on the board to start, Karl-Anthony Towns (22 PTS, 10 RBS) and Jalen Brunson (19 PTS, 4 AST, 3 TO) scored, and we were off. Neither team impressed from deep, combining to make two of their first seven attempts, a trend that continued through the half. Unlike opening night, the whistles were fairly quiet, and the game had a better pace. The villains were pests on the glass, out-rebounding our heroes and turning five O-boards into five extra shots.

After trailing early, the guests used the free throw line to climb into the lead, and the score stayed closed from there. The ‘Bockers goosed their lead to five, and Boston clawed their way back. The bench contributed positive minutes yet again. Landry Shamet (8 PTS) checked in early to relieve a foul-carrying, blank-shooting Mikal Bridges. Also off the bench, Miles McBride (20 PTS, 6-of-8 3pt) took the floor around the six-minute mark. When he fired from the corner, TD Garden let loose a loud “Deeeuuuccceee” and were rewarded with a swish.

Late in the quarter, Anunoby was the only starter on the court, playing alongside Jose Alvarado, McBride, Shamet, and Andre Drummond. Twice we saw Alvarado wrestling a Celtic for the ball on the floor. His dogged defense helped to preserve a 27-26 lead a the break.

New York gave up five points to Luka Garza to start the second and Mike Brown needed a timeout before two minutes had passed. He replaced Andre Drummond with Karl-Anthony Towns. New York fell behind by eight before restoring their composure. At 7:30, Brunson returned to the fray and led Towns, Hart, and Jordan Clarkson led a comeback to tie the score, which was undone by buckets by Tatum and Neemiias Queta.

Robinson returned and continued to putter ineffectively for about six minutes. New Knicks reserve center, James Wiseman, made his season debut for New York with two minutes left in the half and promptly collected a loose ball foul. Fortunately, Josh Hart connected on his first triple of the night (after four tries) and followed that with an off-balance hook, but George knocked down a buzzer-beater for a 50-49 lead.

In the first half, the Knicks made just 30% from deep; Boston was a shade better at 35%. The orange-and-blue crew had taken 12 free throws to their opponent’s four, and each team had 21 boards at the break. In fact, the teams were nearly identical up and down the board. Towns topped all scorers with 12 points and eight rebounds, while Tatum had 11 points on 11 shots.

Anunoby was a bricklayer in the season opener (3-of-12 FG, 1-of-9 3PT), but his second dinger tonight, plus a cutting layup, got New York humming out of halftime. Jordan Walsh, Tatum, and Derrick White went on an 8-0 run before Brunson laced one from deep. In this game of runs, though, it seemed only a matter of time before one team hit the gas and began packing on a significant lead.

Weirdly, through two-and-a-half quarters, Queta was the only Celtic to take free throws—and just six at that. Clean defense so far by Gotham’s greatest!

Spoke too soon. Drummond gave Towns a breather at the five-minute mark and collected two infractions. After McBride picked off Queta and converted back-to-back treys, the Knicks trailed 70-69. Queta seemed hell-bent to prove his value as the Celtics’ center, hitting more free throws and a corner three to reach 12 points and pad his team’s lead. Shamet fouled on a screen, Drummond picked up a technical foul, Hart mishandled a Brunson pass, and the third frame ended with the Knicks down, 83-73.

Robinson punched back in to start the final period. He bodied Anunoby, blocked Towns, and slammed an alley-oop. The crowd went —and then the big fella committed foul number five. Back to the bench with eight-and-a-half to go. Many watching the Amazon Prime stream at home felt a shiver of déjà vu.

While the deficit reached 12, Bridges provided no offensive support. He shot 2-of-8 in the season opener and whiffed on all eight shots in Boston. He has yet to attempt a free throw this year. With production like that, we weren’t surprised when his night finished at 8:25. Meanwhile, McBride had netted 5-of-7 from deep for 23 points and counting with seven minutes remaining. That’ll bring up the team’s overall percentage!

KAT led the league with 56 double-doubles last season. With four minutes left, he grabbed his tenth board for his second double-double of the new campaign, flushed a Brunson miss, and brought the hole to three.

Hart was a shady shooter from downtown, missing five and making two—but that second one was clutch. Then KAT picked Queta’s pocket and Brunson pulled-up to make the score 99-98.

This might have been game two of the season, but it felt like Game 2 of the ECF. Tatum scored on back-to-back jumpers. OG made two freebies. The deficit was three when Tatum— who was on a heater—connected from deep with 30 seconds left. McBride hit his sixth triple at 14 seconds, but the Knicks were forced to foul and pray. Pritchard made one and missed one, and in the resulting fracas, George fouled Brunson. Cap missed a free throw with four seconds left, intentionally bricked the second, and OG missed a futile, final heave. Ballgame.

Quoth Good names all taken, “I took the over at 58. Still alive.” The season is young, the sky is not falling. After a short offseason and the usual rust, the Knicks have lost two close contests against playoff teams. Our heroes head home to host the O’Magic on Sunday, which should have a more favorable outcome. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

title: How F1's top four teams are comparing in Austin
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
Formula 1's United States Grand Prix looks poised to be a multi-team fight for victory based on how the top four teams have started at Austin.

Here are the early clues about the pecking order, with single-lap and long-run pace trends painting very different pictures.

The combination of the varying strengths of the leading cars and the wide range of corner speeds of the Austin circuit that tests every facet of a car means that Ferrari, Red Bull and Mercedes, which were separated by less than two tenths on single-lap pace, all excelled and struggled at different parts of the track.

Pacesetter Charles Leclerc was strongest in the slow corners. He carried the highest minimum speed at Turn 1, matched Kimi Antonelli's best at Turn 12, and braked late for the Turn 11 hairpin without compromising his exit. He was often first back on the throttle.

In the high-speed sections, Leclerc was quickest through Turns 6-7, keeping part-throttle where Max Verstappen lifted - however, at times the picture in the fast corners was muddied by deployment variations. As always, the Ferrari lost significant time on the straights - just over six tenths relative to Verstappen.

Verstappen's Red Bull was mighty on the straights, gaining around six tenths on Leclerc once the speeds had settled, and a little over a tenth compared to the Mercedes. That characteristic also gave him a strong start to the lap down the start/finish straight. He was committed on the brakes in terms of stopping power, but was often later on the throttle at slow-corner exits, with that approach paying off at Turn 20, where he had a strong exit.

Where Red Bull is lacking most for Verstappen was obvious after a pretty good day left the four-time F1 world champion seeking a finer balance rather than anything drastic.

"It's clearly the low-speed performance that we are focused on at the moment," was Red Bull technical director Pierre Wache's verdict when asked by The Race if there was a standout area to improve overnight.

"Low speed is the key for us."

That aforementioned Verstappen preference for braking slightly earlier, but harder, to prioritise a good exit was clear throughout the lap but, other than at Turn 20, it did not really manifest in laptime due to the Red Bull seemingly lacking rotation.

Verstappen's Turn 1 was the worst of the top three. Despite braking earliest he was slowest back to full throttle - due to some wheelspin he had to manage - and swung from just over a tenth up on Leclerc to 0.25s behind.

Turn 12 was his other big loss, around 0.2s again. Despite again braking earlier, Verstappen did not have the response he needed when he initially started applying steering lock into the corner and ran a little deep, dropping his minimum speed 10km/h below Leclerc's and Antonelli's.

It's possible the Red Bull is not quite as compliant on the bumps in the braking zones here, which is contributing to Verstappen braking slightly earlier and not being as attacking or as confident on entry, or as steady on exit.

"Finding the right balance was more difficult than expected," Wache admitted.

Where Mercedes and McLaren fit in

Antonelli's Mercedes had a more balanced performance profile: quicker on the straights than the Ferrari but not at Red Bull level, but showing good speed on the approach to the hairpin. Potentially, that reflected differences in deployment.

He was strong in Turns 8-9, Turn 15 and Turn 12, but did lose out in several corners on the exits.

McLaren's single-lap pace also looked nowhere on the timesheets, with Lando Norris the faster of its drivers in FP2 but 1.082s off the pace. However, this time was set on hards as he had to abort both of his qualifying simulation laps.

The first was because of a snap mid-corner at Turn 9, possibly the result of running in turbulent air caused by George Russell's Mercedes ahead. His second lap, on soft Pirellis now past their best, was abandoned after a lockup at Turn 15.

"We set a purple [fastest sector time] in FP2 as well, we just didn't finish the lap," said McLaren chief technical officer Rob Marshall. "It was a competitive lap up until the point where we made a mistake.

"Going forward from here we've got to be quite optimistic really."

That first sector time was the fastest at the time he set it, and although it was eclipsed by Verstappen that was only by 0.015s - and it was faster than anything achieved by Ferrari or Mercedes.

On the raw numbers, Norris's McLaren was fastest on the long-run averages in FP2, but it's a confusing picture for a number of reasons.

Traffic affected a number of drivers' long runs and all three tyre compounds were used, so it's tricky to compare a nine-lap Norris run on durable hards to Verstappen's 11-lap soft-tyre run, for example.

But Norris's strong long run backs up McLaren looking stronger than the FP2 result suggested.

Pirelli expects the hard tyre to "play only a limited role in defining race strategies", with a one-stop using the softs and mediums most likely.

Verstappen's soft tyres held up impressively well with consistent laptimes and less of a drop-off compared to Leclerc's.

Team-mate Isack Hadjar was clearly not as comfortable. He struggled with overheating front tyres all day; "it's just a disaster" he said of his soft tyre lap.

"It was just undriveable, and I was losing the front end massively. We need to have a look because that's not normal, why there is so much deg on one lap."

Hadjar said his tyres were "completely killed" in the high-speed corners. Red Bull's Wache said this was key to the difference as he said Hadjar and Verstappen weren't far apart on set-up.

Lewis Hamilton, George Russell, Oscar Piastri and Hadjar all appear to have started the weekend a step behind their respective team-mates.

Hamilton said he "tried a different direction with the set-up, but I wasn't comfortable in the car, especially over the bumps", while Piastri's long run pace on the softs appeared to sharply tail off.

That picture may alter as teams learn overnight lessons and change set-up and deployment patterns, but right now all four teams look like they are in the hunt at Austin.

title: What was behind one F1 team's strangest day of 2026
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
Williams had a peculiar Friday at the United States Grand Prix as it ended practice with its fastest Formula 1 car slower than Cadillac and the other 8.1 seconds off the pace.

Alex Albon was an exaggerated slowest in FP2 (just as he was in FP1) but the team's real pace was still disappointing, with Carlos Sainz even behind Valtteri Bottas's Cadillac.

A track-limits deletion was behind Albon's particularly unusual deficit and the strangest Friday of 2026 was partly down to Williams sacrificing typical in-weekend work for 2027 development help in FP1.

This meant aero testing on hards in FP1 followed by a short medium-tyre run, as Williams chief trackside engineer Paul Williams said the team had "balanced off performance for this weekend versus long-term learning" because "this track's very good for aero data collection".

Sainz said: "We decided to invest FP1 on a track that we knew we were going to be weak [on] to understand how to basically map the car in order to learn from this year's car as much as possible for next year's car.

"We know we have a lot of weaknesses on this year's car on a track like this and we want to make sure we understand it and we map it to try and get it right next year in the windtunnel."

Then the focus in FP2 was a more standard Friday plan just with a heavier emphasis on high-fuel running as Williams knows its one-lap pace is likely to be lacking anyway - although its long-run pace looked weak in the midfield too.

The Circuit of the Americas is a punishing track as its layout comprises a mix of medium- and high-speed sweeps, long-duration corners, and bumpy heavy braking zones.

This exposes a lot of Williams's underlying weaknesses of recent years and the specific shortcomings of its 2026 car.

In FP2, shortly after Sainz complained the car was a mess and he had no confidence in the rear, Albon reported zero confidence under braking.

"When you have no downforce you're going to suffer either on braking or on high speed," said Sainz.

"We know this year we lack a lot of downforce in the car and especially when it gets bumpy, when it gets high speed, when it gets hot, when it gets windy - like it gets in COTA - the only thing that saves you is downforce and that's what we don't have on this year's car.

"So we're working on it, we are braced for a tough weekend, don't expect any miracles, but at least we are investing in learning as much as possible for next year."

title: Winners and losers from COTA's Friday F1 action
author: Ben Anderson
text:
After a triple-header of races, which culminated in a condensed sprint weekend - followed by a weekend off, Formula 1 teams should be delighted to be back to a typical three-practice weekend.

Only, most of them aren't, because the difficult of setting ride-height correctly on this bumpy circuit on a weekend of so many upgrades and car tweaks has made for a lot of grumpy people in the paddock.

Here's our winners and losers from the practice day.

Loser: Lando Norris (7th)

Sounds as though there might be a bit of a disconnect here between how McLaren feels its Austin Friday went and how its world champion driver feels its Austin Friday went.

Lando Norris was properly quick in FP1, within 0.25s of the pace, and in the FP2 long runs looked reasonable, but the qualifying simulations were a disaster - so much so that he actually went slower (by just under a tenth) in FP2 than he managed in FP1.

The major caveat is that big lock-up Norris had at Turn 15, which came shortly after he’d set the best second sector time of all.

But this is at the crux of it all really. There’s no doubt the McLaren can be a fast car, Norris just maintains it’s “very difficult to drive” and too much on a knife’s edge to be able to readily access that level of performance.

“Like it has been for a long time, it's just too difficult to be able to be consistent, to get a nice feeling consistently,” he added. “The pace is not bad, it's just very difficult to achieve it.

“To get the car to be quick, we just have to try so hard to be perfect, and you cannot be perfect. I'm sure everyone has similar problems in a way, but we're just not quick enough yet, easily, to be there consistently.”

Winner: McLaren (7th & 8th)

What on earth is McLaren doing in our winners' section when Norris was so downbeat and both cars ended FP2 behind a Racing Bulls, you ask?

That's down to the mood higher up at McLaren, which seems a whole lot brighter than Norris's outlook.

Chief technical officer Rob Marshall spoke of the "really small parts" that McLaren has brought to Austin offering a "measurable benefit" that also made a noticeable laptime difference.

That measurable benefit has included an aerodynamic gain with its brake changes, including flow conditioning around the wheels and wake control.

All that led Marshall to conclude that McLaren is in the fight with its main rivals here.

"Going forward from here we've got to be quite optimistic really," he said.

Winner: Charles Leclerc/Ferrari (1st)

An obvious choice of course, considering he topped both Friday sessions, but Leclerc didn’t just look rapid on the soft tyre in FP2.

It looked as though that pace came readily to hand, and the fact he was over six tenths clear of Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton - who had two stabs at a qualifying simulation and set roughly the same lap time on each go - suggests it’s Leclerc in particular who’s got things hooked up for Ferrari in the early phase of this weekend.

The big proviso is the long-run pace, where usually Ferrari would feel its inherent strength lies this season. Has Leclerc’s rapid one-lap speed come at too much of a compromise for tyre degradation? And of course, the perennial question of whether Ferrari can keep up the pace when the engines get turned up for Saturday’s qualifying showdown.

"I think we started the weekend on the right foot with a good balance and I think that is probably the outstanding thing for this Friday," Leclerc said.

"But I also believe the others will start pushing a bit more their cars as they always do coming [into] quali, and so it's going to be tough because it's been a very clean Friday on my side.

"There's more performance in the car, a little bit more, but the others seems to be gaining more than us from the Friday to the Saturday, and seeing the little gap there is... it's not going to be so easy tomorrow."

Winner: Aston Martin (16th & 17th)

Chief trackside officer Mike Krack spoke on Thursday of a need to "manage your expectations a little bit better" in the wake of Aston Martin's misplaced Singapore GP confidence. Fernando Alonso, meanwhile, was quietly talking up the chances of "nice surprises" at the US GP.

Based on Friday practice, Alonso was right to have some optimism. Inside the theoretical Q2 cutoff in both sessions (and up in the dizzying heights of 12th in FP1), with team-mate Lance Stroll for company both times, the Aston Martin looks like a genuine midfield contender again.

Yes, that's still a sign of how the mighty have fallen for a team that so much is expected of, on a day where Adrian Newey spoke of the disappointment Honda was likely to be feeling over its 2026 F1 engine progress .

But in the context of this painful campaign, this was one of the more painless Fridays.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (9th)

OK, run plans, fuel loads and especially at COTA, lap deletions all play a part, but Isack Hadjar failed to get within a second of his Red Bull team-mate Max Verstappen in either practice and called his car's handling disgusting.

Asked to explain his "disgusting" radio comments after practice, Hadjar said "it's just a disaster".

He explained: "From sector one to the end of the lap, I was slower [on the softs] than on the medium. It was just undrivable and I was losing the front end massively. We need to have a look because that's not normal, why is there so much deg on one lap?"

Asking the journalists certainly won't provide the answer, Isack...

Loser: Williams (20th & 22nd)

After being the first team to blatantly and vocally switch its focus from 2025 to get ready for 2026, to be among the first teams to do that two years in a row is the most almighty of damning indictments for where Williams is at.

It was so sure its car would be terrible at Austin that it ran an unusual strategy of compromising this weekend competitively to try to learn how to fix the issues it's having with its handling.

Even Aston Martin - well over four seconds off the pace at the start of the season - didn't admit a switch of focus to 2027, and basically built a new car, which by some stats could have been on pole for the last two races with a different engine.

Anyway, if ruining this weekend gives Williams a huge insight into its troubles for next year, of course it will be worth it it. Until then, it has to suffer the indignity of very publicly having to admit defeat with a 2026 car it was supposed to have a great headstart with.

Winner: Liam Lawson (6th)

Liam Lawson managed to jump both McLarens in FP2, and while that's unlikely on Sunday and perhaps as much down to what was going on with McLaren, it's still a sign the Racing Bulls is working well.

Lawson says "overall the car is in a good place" and that it's "nice to see it working" given the "new stuff" on the car.

More deg than expected and a likely resurgent Nico Hulkenberg - whose Audi team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto beat the Racing Bulls in FP1 but has a grid penalty on Sunday, while Hulkenberg only got new parts in FP2 and is expecting a driveability fix on Saturday - means Lawson isn't out of the woods yet.

And we've seen on more than one occasion this year a Racing Bulls produce an excellent practice lap which doesn't translate into race performance. But that being said, Friday was a good day for Lawson.

Winner: Cadillac (19th & 21st)

No, this isn't based on Valtteri Bottas's 19th place in FP2 ahead of both Williams. But it is based on the way he characterised the day.

"I think we've got the most done that we've ever done in one Friday," said Bottas, who called this something of a test day - but one that ran smoothly and better than expected.

Cadillac still expects this to be a tough weekend; degradation and tyre heating, as Bottas put it, is "definitely not our strength" and that was apparent on Friday. And Cadillac's productiveness also means "it's going to be a busy evening, because like I said with both cars we've tried a lot of different things". (Team-mate Sergio Perez ran an experimental floor, with 2027 in mind, while Bottas ran different front wings and tried different roll stiffnesses.)

Those experimental ideas (which Colton Herta also ran in FP1) were done "to challenge our thinking on the aero concept of the car", as per chief racing officer Marc Hynes, as well as to validate the correlation between Cadillac's CFD and windtunnel work and what it's seeing in the real world.

Based on this reception, it's been a positive Friday's work.

title: Embattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made public
author: Sarah Basford Canales
text:
WA politician says he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be ‘unacceptable’

Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast

Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator releases a letter detailing the allegations against him.

After days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, Steele-John posted a statement to social media late Friday night.

In the statement, the Western Australian senator said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”. He will instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.

“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.

Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” are made had now been set.

“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.

The 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with the party’s leader, David Shoebridge , over whether he was on leave while an investigation was undertaken into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.

The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission .

Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.

The three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.

The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear and backlash. The letter provided no further detail.

In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025.

Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.

“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.

Steele-John was defiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday , rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.

Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch had released the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.

Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.

title: MotoGP Australian GP: Marquez takes pole in wet qualifying despite crash
Marquez falls on his way to staggering Phillip Island MotoGP pole
author: Matt Beer
text:
Marc Marquez took pole for MotoGP's Australian Grand Prix by a staggering 1.5 seconds at a wet Phillip Island, despite crashing on his first Q2 lap.

With fresh rain falling as Q2 began, that low-side crash into the Miller corner looked like it might leave Marquez a disastrous 12th on the grid.

But he managed to remount his Ducati, the rain eased again, and with the track to himself for his next lap Marquez jumped to pole.

Rain ace Johann Zarco had been fastest at first and did take provisional pole back from Marquez for a while on the next runs.

Then Marquez utterly blew everyone else away on the last laps of the session though, putting in a 1m34.203s that was an astonishing 1.494s faster than the eventual second-place rider, his brother Alex on the Gresini Ducati.

Zarco kept his LCR Honda on the front row in third.

Marquez's title rival Jorge Martin never looked like he had pole pace in the damp but making it back up to fourth on the grid with his last lap counts as a very good save considering Marquez's pace.

Martin's long-shot championship contender Aprilia team-mate Marco Bezzecchi didn't manage that - he starts only ninth for the weekend's two races.

Home hero Jack Miller was fastest in Q1 and briefly had a provisional front row in Q2 before ending up a still heartwarming fifth for Pramac Yamaha.

Performances varied in the conditions, with Marquez's astonishing pole at one end of the field in stark contrast to how far off the pace tail end pair Fabio Quartararo and Franco Morbidelli were in 19th and 20th on the reduced grid that will lack any factory Hondas following the unwell Luca Marini's withdrawal.

title: Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack
author: Adeshola Ore
text:
Independent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospital

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.

The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.

“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.

Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.

The MP’s husband, Phil Haines, provided an update at the Alfred hospital on Wednesday, saying “both her heart and her mind are in good shape .”

“I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind,” he said.

“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”

Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.

Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.

On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday. “What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.

“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”

Haines’ staff said they had been overwhelmed with kindness shown by the local community in Indi and across Australia and the globe. They said more than $730,000 had been raised for Save the Children in Haines’ honour after her husband directed people to donate to the special appeal as his wife recovered.

“We are deeply moved by the extraordinary generosity of so many people,” the post read.

The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debat, security risks for MPs and mental health services in regional Victoria.

WA Police charged a 56-year-old man after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the the state’s local government minister, Hannah Beazley, days after the alleged attack on Haines.

A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.

Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.

title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
text:
The US is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, with the White House saying on Friday it was working to "protect the economic prosperity and national security of the American people".

The exemptions could also boost Republican candidates in the midterms elections on 3 November, as many US voters list affordability and economic pressures as top issues.

Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race in Maine to keep her seat in the election, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.

After trade talks collapsed this summer, the US and Canada started an escalating tariff war that has affected both sides of the border.

The White House, in a statement, said that starting 30 October the US would remove certain products from the list of Canadian goods it taxes, such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes.

It added those items would be replaced with certain valves, carpets, waste products, among others .

The White House said the action reflects President Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade", as well as "offsetting the burden and disadvantage on U.S. commerce from Canada's discriminatory treatment".

The BBC has contacted the White House, US commerce department and trade representative for further comment.

Also on Friday, President Donald Trump said that Canada is "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday that Canada is open to a mutually beneficial deal, but is willing to wait it out.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said, according to CBC.

Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met with members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

So far, Canada has not commented on the White House's announcement.

LeBlanc's office did not immediately respond on Friday to the BBC's request for comment.

The Wall Street Journal had reported that the exemptions, largely focused on Canadian agricultural and forestry, were made in a bid to help Collins and other Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections.

The reductions could be offset by raising levies on ​other Canadian goods, the Journal reported.

In a statement Collins put out before the White House announcement, the incumbent lawmaker, who is trying to clinch her sixth term, said she had "secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".

"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," she posted on X.

Collins said she has asked US officials and senior administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada.

​Maine's economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the month-long trade war.

title: Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change
author: Guardian staff and agencies
text:
US secretary of state makes comments after Trump tells US rally warships could intervene on return from Iran

Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.

The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.

The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.

Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.

“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Havana on Friday mocked the “desperation” of the US following the comments made by Rubio and Trump.

“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.

“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”

Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.

In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.

Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.

Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.

“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.

“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”

Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.

During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.

Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”

Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.

Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
text:
Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.

The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.

But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.

Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.

And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.

Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.

But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries?

One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate.

The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.

On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries.

And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes.

If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.

Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care

State pension likely to top £13,000 a year

What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?

But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows.

However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.

So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK?

Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund.

But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.

Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.

And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes).

Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing.

As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.

So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap.

The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.

It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men.

But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.

Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.

So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere.

But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action.

The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.

That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
text:
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.

As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.

The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.

"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."

The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.

"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.

"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."

The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says

The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).

Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.

The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.

It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.

This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.

It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.

There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.

But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.
